Characteristic losses like these are used to help identify molecular structures. The spectra of linear alkanes (see Section 7.2), for example, have a series of peaks separated by 14 amu due to the loss of CH2 groups. Common fragmentation patterns for cy- clic alkanes include the loss of side groups, for example methyl at 15 amu, and the elimination of CH2CH2 groups as ethylene, producing a peak at M 2 28, where M is the mass of the molecular ion. A common frag- mentation mechanism for alcohols (see Section 7.6) is the elimination of water to produce an M 2 1 peak. Finally, the mass spectra of molecules with π bonds of- ten show prominent molecular ion peaks because the bond in the resulting ion is still quite strong and the molecular ion quite stable.

Polypeptides typically fragment by cleaving peptide bonds as shown by the dashed lines in the figure. The peak at M 2 17 is due to the loss of either 3OH or 3NH3 and the peaks at lower masses arise from cleav- age of one or more peptide bonds. The M 1 1 and M 1 23 peaks arise from proton or sodium ion attachment. High-resolution mass spectrometry provides not only accurate molecular weights but, perhaps more im- portantly, molecular formulas. The molecules CO, N2, CH2N and C2H2 all have nominal masses of 28 amu and are indistinguishable at low resolution. The precise masses of 12C16O, 14N2, 12C1H2

14N and 12C2 1H2 (see Table 19.1) are actually 27.9949, 28.0062, 28.0187 and 28.0312 amu, respectively, are readily separated at high resolution (1 part per 104 2 106 is common). More complicated molecules have significantly more possi- bilities than this but measuring exact masses alone at high resolution is sufficient to determine molecular for- mulas uniquely, supplanting chemical methods such as combustion analysis (see Figure 2.3) which is now used primarily to establish the purity of newly synthesized compounds.
